title: Perf CI flamegraph and trace collectors — working notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects the recommended tooling, quick scripts, and CI job templates we use to generate flamegraphs and traces for the serving runtime. It is meant for on-call triage, perf CI jobs, and periodic regressions.

Goals:
- Make perf data production- and CI-collectable with low overhead.
- Standardize naming/retention and upload location for trace artifacts.
- Provide actionable runbook steps for common bottlenecks (CPU hot loops, allocation spikes, syscall waits, scheduling).
- Keep a minimal set of commands that any engineer can run without diving into infra.

Scope:
- CPU sampling flamegraphs (perf, py-spy, go pprof)
- eBPF traces (bcc / bpftrace) for syscall/wake latency and scheduling
- CI job templates to produce artifacts and upload to S3/Artifact store
- Quick triage checklist for interpreting a flamegraph and deciding remediation

Prereqs / baseline environment:
- Linux kernels 5.4+ recommended for bpf tooling.
- perf installed on images (apt: linux-perf or linux-tools-common / linux-tools-$(uname -r)).
- py-spy for Python stacks (pip install py-spy).
- Go binaries built with -gcflags="-N -l" for accurate pprof (if applicable).
- FlameGraph perl scripts available in PATH (https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph).

Artifact naming and storage convention:
- s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/{service}/{branch_or_tag}/{commit}/{job}/{YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS}-{type}.{ext}
- type: flame (svg), folded (txt), trace (json), perf.data (raw)
- Keep artifacts for 90 days by default; critical-release runs 1 year.

Quick commands (native perf):
- Record 30s system-wide sampling at 99Hz and produce flamegraph:
  sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30
  sudo perf script > out.perf
  ./stackcollapse-perf.pl out.perf > out.folded
  ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
- If you can run against a single PID:
  sudo perf record -F 99 -p <PID> -g -- sleep 30

Python (py-spy) — lower overhead and no root required for many cases:
- Record a flamegraph of a running python process:
  py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <PID> --rate 100 --duration 30
- Record a raw flame format that can be collapsed later:
  py-spy record -o profile.raw --pid <PID> --format raw --duration 30

Go (pprof) — if server exposes /debug/pprof/profile:
- curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > cpu.pb
- go tool pprof -svg ./binary cpu.pb > cpu.svg

eBPF traces (bcc / bpftrace) — useful for syscalls, wakeups, scheduling issues:
- syscall latency example using bpftrace one-liner (root):
  sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read { @start[tid] = nsecs; } tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /@start[tid]/ { @lat = hist(nsecs - @start[tid]); delete(@start[tid]); }'
- sched switch sampling (high overhead):
  sudo bpftrace -e 'profile:hz:99 /comm == "server-binary"/ { @[comm, pid] = count(); }'

CI job template (GitHub Actions snippet) — produces artifacts and uploads to S3:
name: perf-benchmark-flamegraph
on: [push, workflow_dispatch]
jobs:
  flamegraph:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build runtime
        run: make build-server # adjust for repo
      - name: Start test binary in background
        run: ./bin/server --test-mode & echo $! > /tmp/server.pid
      - name: Wait for warmup
        run: sleep 10
      - name: Capture perf
        run: sudo perf record -F 99 -p $(cat /tmp/server.pid) -g -- sleep 30
      - name: Generate flamegraph
        run: sudo perf script > out.perf && ./stackcollapse-perf.pl out.perf > out.folded && ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
      - name: Upload artifact to S3
        env:
          AWS_S3_BUCKET: redwood-perf-artifacts
          S3_PREFIX: ${{ github.ref_name }}/$GITHUB_SHA/perf-artifacts
        run: |
          aws s3 cp flame.svg s3://$AWS_S3_BUCKET/$S3_PREFIX/flame.svg --acl bucket-owner-full-control
          aws s3 cp out.folded s3://$AWS_S3_BUCKET/$S3_PREFIX/out.folded --acl bucket-owner-full-control

Notes on CI job design and cost:
- Keep sample durations short (15–60s) to limit runner costs. For regression runs, schedule longer runs in dedicated perf workers.
- Use reserved self-hosted runners for zero-noise baselines if available.
- Record raw perf.data only for failing runs; upload folded traces by default.

Runbook: Triage flow when a P99 regression is observed
1) Grab the perf artifact for the failing job / roll (S3 path). If none, trigger a repro CI run with --perf-collect.
2) Open flame.svg. Look for broad stacks vs narrow hot functions.
   - Broad stacks with many children often indicate increased system time or blocking (I/O, GC).
   - A single tall stack usually points to a tight CPU hotspot.
3) If the top frame is kernel (e.g., futex_wait, epoll_wait), check thread states and trace syscalls. Use bpftrace to sample syscalls.
4) If Python-heavy, check allocations: py-spy has --native to show C extensions. Consider heapy/tracemalloc if allocations suspected.
5) If GC suspected (Go): correlate pprof tracers (goroutine/block/counts) and check GOGC settings.
6) If NUMA or NVMe stalls suspected, check iostat, dmesg, and perf top -p for cycles lost in iowait.
7) Add a repro microbenchmark and run locally under perf to confirm.
8) Open a bug with reproducer, attach folded trace and flame.svg, mark severity and suspected subsystem.

Common gotchas and tips:
- perf requires matching kernel headers for symbolization with some distros. Keep the perf-tools version pinned on runners.
- For containers, sampling requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN or using a privileged runner. Use self-hosted runners for low-friction captures.
- Inline functions and optimized builds make stacks noisy. For deep insight, build with frame pointers or disable inlining for targeted components.
- Systrace vs user-space sampling: when in doubt, collect both perf.record + strace for short duration to see syscalls.

Sample helper scripts (put in tools/perf):
- collect-perf.sh (bash)
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -euo pipefail
  PID=$1
  DURATION=${2:-30}
  OUTDIR=${3:-/tmp/perf-$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)}
  mkdir -p $OUTDIR
  sudo perf record -F 99 -p $PID -g -- sleep $DURATION
  sudo perf script > $OUTDIR/out.perf
  ./stackcollapse-perf.pl $OUTDIR/out.perf > $OUTDIR/out.folded
  ./flamegraph.pl $OUTDIR/out.folded > $OUTDIR/flame.svg
  echo "Artifacts: $OUTDIR"

- upload-to-s3.sh (bash)
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -euo pipefail
  BUCKET=$1
  PREFIX=$2
  FILES=("$3")
  for f in "${FILES[@]}"; do
    aws s3 cp "$f" "s3://$BUCKET/$PREFIX/$(basename $f)" --acl bucket-owner-full-control
  done

Interpretation checklist (quick):
- CPU-bound: tall user function; optimize algorithm or offload to async work.
- Lock contention: look for futex or top stack showing locks; add finer-grained locks or reduce shared state.
- Syscall wait: epoll_wait/futex/recvfrom at top → investigate network or event loop saturation.
- GC/alloc: many small allocations in stacks; consider object pooling or faster allocators.

Next steps / To-do:
- Wire up a scheduled weekly perf baseline job on main branch that stores artifacts for trend analysis.
- Add a small set of synthetic workloads (small/medium/large seq-length) to CI perf jobs for regression detection.
- Build a lightweight UI to compare flamegraphs (diffing folded stacks) — prototype in perf-tools repo.

References and cheatsheets:
- FlameGraph repo: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
- py-spy: https://github.com/benfred/py-spy
- bpftrace one-liners: https://github.com/iovisor/bpftrace/tree/master/tools
- Perf tutorial: https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page

Notes to self:
- Revisit perf runner image to include correct linux-tools for all active kernel versions we ship.
- Check with infra about permissions for privileged self-hosted runners for scheduled perf collection.
